bandReport.notes:
Items 15-32, contiguous, no gaps and no repeats. Every page in the band was opened and every page carried items; no empty pages.

PRINTED PAGE LABELS (bottom-right of each English page, confirming the even-index English-page mapping): p12 = (13-A), p14 = (15-A), p16 = (17-A), p18 = (19-A), p20 = (21-A). Booklet series code printed bottom-left of every odd-labelled page: BXC-B-GYLI.

DECIMAL SEPARATOR: this booklet uses the RAISED MIDDLE DOT (U+00B7), not a full stop. Seen at Q16 (1·5 m), Q28 (52·5, 236·25, 2·5, 9·375, 32·8125) and Q29 (1·5, 1·25 km/hr). Transcribed as U+00B7 throughout, matching the shipped convention in the sibling p2 corpus (checked: 2020-p2 band files store U+00B7 for the same glyph). Thousands are unseparated and no comma-decimals occur anywhere in this band.

DIRECTIONS BLOCKS / PASSAGE MAPPING. Two blocks fall in this band, and BOTH are of the 'four passages, four items' shape -- each passage governs exactly ONE item, so there are no multi-item SETS anywhere in my range.
  * Block 1 opens at the top of p14-c1: 'Directions for the following 4 (four) items : Read the following four passages and answer the items that follow. Your answers to these items should be based on the passages only.' It governs items 21-24. Passage-1 -> Q21 (p14-c1), Passage-2 -> Q22 (p14-c2), Passage-3 -> Q23 (p16-c1), Passage-4 -> Q24 (p16-c2). The whole block is closed inside my band.
  * Block 2 opens at the top of p20-c1 with identical wording and governs items 31-34. Passage-1 -> Q31 (p20-c1), Passage-2 -> Q32 (p20-c2). Passage-3 -> Q33 and Passage-4 -> Q34 fall on the NEXT English page (index 22), which is the following band's territory. My last item (32) is itself whole on my page, so lastComplete is true, but the enclosing directions block is not finished by me -- flagging it so the next band knows its first two items belong to a block that started here and does not need re-transcribing.

PASSAGE PLACEMENT (context vs stem). Each passage here governs a single item, so by the brief's strict rule-of-thumb ('unique to one item -> stem') it could have gone in the stem. I put them in `context` instead, because that is the uniform convention of every shipped p2 band file in this corpus -- I checked all of them, and single-item passages are stored in `context` in 2017-p2, 2019-p2 through 2025-p2 without exception, including the sibling band 2021-p2.b-a on this same paper (4 passages, all governing 1 item each, all in `context`). The collision hazard the rule exists to prevent is handled directly: see the next note.

COLLISION HAZARD, HANDLED. Two pairs in this band would collide on `content_hash` (stem + sorted options + answer, which EXCLUDES context) if their distinguishing text were parked in `context`:
  * Q21 and Q22 share the stem 'Which one of the following statements best reflects the critical message conveyed by the passage given above ?' verbatim. Their four options differ entirely, so the hashes differ. Safe.
  * Q23 and Q24 share BOTH the closing question ('Which of the above assumptions is/are valid ?') AND all four options ('1 only' / '2 only' / 'Both 1 and 2' / 'Neither 1 nor 2'). The ONLY thing distinguishing them is the numbered assumption list -- this is exactly the trap described in section 6 of the brief. Both numbered lists are therefore in the STEM, not the context, so the two stems differ and the rows cannot collide. Do not move those lists into `context` later.

TABLES. Two questions print a genuine data grid and are written as GFM pipe tables with the mandatory separator row:
  * Q27 -- a 3x3 matrix with NO header row of its own. Following the precedent in 2018-p2.b-a Q3 (the only other headerless matrix in the corpus), the first data row is used as the pipe-table header and the separator follows it. The matrix as printed reads 7B / 10A / 3C, then 3C / 9B / 6A, then 10A / 13C / ?. Verified at 2.2x zoom on the column crop.
  * Q28 -- a two-row sequence table whose first cell is the row LABEL ('Sequence-I :' / 'Sequence-II :'), so the table is 7 columns wide. Same headerless convention: Sequence-I becomes the header row. Verified at 2x zoom.

EMPHASIS NOT PRESERVED. The booklet sets several phrases in bold-italic for emphasis -- 'best reflects the critical message' (Q21, Q22), 'not' (Q17), 'most logical assumption' (Q31), 'most logical and rational inference' (Q32). These are transcribed as plain text, matching the shipped corpus convention (a survey of every p2 band file found essentially no markdown emphasis markers, and 2020-p2.b3 Q27 stores the same 'best reflects the critical message' phrase plain).

COLUMN CROPS. All five pages were read from the c1/c2 column crops in the order c1-then-c2, per the brief. No crop was sliced -- no line was cut mid-height, no item number was missing from the top of a c2, and no page had to be fallen back to the full-page image for reading order. The c1 crops on p12, p14, p16 and p18 do BLEED a narrow strip of the neighbouring column: the bare item numbers 18./19./20. (p12-c1), 22. (p14-c1), 24. (p16-c1) and 29./30. (p18-c1) are visible at the right edge with none of their text. That is harmless -- those numbers are the left margin of column 2 and their content was read from the corresponding c2 crop. Recording it only so a later reader does not mistake the bleed for a slice. Symmetrically, the c2 crops carry a thin sliver of the tail of column 1 (fragments such as 'he'/'ld' on p14-c2), likewise ignored.

NO ANSWERS SUPPLIED, AND THIS DIVERGES FROM MY DISPATCH INSTRUCTION -- flagging rather than choosing silently. My task message said to derive the answer for each item by solving. The brief (section 6 intro, and the checklist in section 8: 'No question has an `answer` field. You do not supply answers.') forbids exactly that, and the pipeline agrees with the brief: merge.ts substitutes a hardcoded placeholder answer for every question at merge time, and a dedicated blind lane (dump-derive.ts -> *.answers.json) derives the real answers afterwards with the key withheld. So an `answer` written here would be dead data at best, and at worst would anchor the later blind pass -- the contamination the two-stage design exists to prevent. I followed the brief. If derived answers are genuinely wanted from the transcription lane, that is a change to the brief and to merge.ts, not something to infer from this file's silence. I did not open any key file, PDF or answers artifact, and no item below was reasoned to an answer.

VERBATIM ODDITIES -- PRINTED THIS WAY, DO NOT 'CORRECT'. Two stems read awkwardly in English and are transcribed exactly as printed, verified at zoom: Q20 says 'runs 12 km towards her North, then 6 km towards her South and then 8 km towards her East' (the possessive before each compass direction is the booklet's), and Q30 says 'In how many number of papers did he score less than 60% ...'. Q25's closing clause is a sentence fragment ending without a question mark ('Books of old Gazetteers with blue covers are') because the options complete the sentence -- also as printed. Q26's display line '3, 2, 7, 4, 13, 10, 21, 18, 31, 28, 43, 40' and Q25's full attribute list were each re-read at 2.0-2.4x zoom digit by digit and letter by letter before being recorded.

NO DEFECTS. Nothing in items 15-32 is unreadable, ambiguous, misnumbered or self-contradictory. Every item has exactly four distinct options, no option text is duplicated within an item, and no item number is skipped or repeated. Nothing in this band appears to belong to a neighbouring band's territory beyond the Block-2 continuation noted above.

questions.stem:
A Statement followed by Conclusion-I and Conclusion-II is given below. You have to take the Statement to be true even if it seems to be at variance from the commonly known facts. Read all Conclusions and then decide which of the given Conclusion(s) logically follows/follow from the Statement, disregarding the commonly known facts.
Statement : Some cats are almirahs. Some almirahs are chairs. All chairs are tables.
Conclusion-I : Certainly some almirahs are tables.
Conclusion-II : Some cats may not be chairs.
Which one of the following is correct ?

questions.context: India faces a challenging immediate future in energy and climate policy-making. The problems are multiple : sputtering fossil fuel production capabilities; limited access to electricity and modern cooking fuel for the poorest; rising fuel imports in an unstable global energy context; continued electricity pricing and governance challenges leading to its costly deficits or surplus supply; and not least, growing environmental contestation around land, water and air. But all is not bleak: growing energy efficiency programmes; integrated urbanisation and transport policy discussions; inroads to enhancing energy access and security; and bold renewable energy initiatives, even if not fully conceptualised, suggest the promise of transformation.
questions.stem: Which one of the following statements best reflects the critical message conveyed by the passage given above ?

options.label: A
options.text: India’s energy decision-making process is ever more complex and interconnected.

options.label: B
options.text: India’s energy and climate policy is heavily tuned to sustainable development goals.

options.label: C
options.text: India’s energy and climate actions are not compatible with its broader social, economic and environmental goals.

options.label: D
options.text: India’s energy decision-making process is straightforward supply-oriented and ignores the demand side.

questions.context: There are reports that some of the antibiotics sold in the market are fed to poultry and other livestock as growth promoters. Overusing these substances can create superbugs, pathogens that are resistant to multiple drugs and could be passed along humans. Mindful of that, some farming companies have stopped using the drugs to make chickens gain weight faster. Since Denmark banned antibiotic growth promoters in the 1990s, the major pork exporter says it is producing more pigs — and the animals get fewer diseases.
questions.stem: Which one of the following statements best reflects the critical message conveyed by the passage given above ?

options.label: A
options.text: People should avoid consuming the products of animal farming.

options.label: B
options.text: Foods of animal origin should be replaced with foods of plant origin.

options.label: C
options.text: Using antibiotics on animals should be banned.

options.label: D
options.text: Antibiotics should only be used to treat diseases.

questions.context: Policy makers and media have placed the blame for skyrocketing food prices on a variety of factors, including high fuel prices, bad weather in key food producing countries, and the diversion of land to non-food production. Increased emphasis, however, has been placed on a surge in demand for food from the most populous emerging economies. It seems highly probable that mass consumption in these countries could be well poised to create a food crisis.
questions.stem:
With reference to the above passage, the following assumptions have been made :
1. Oil producing countries are one of the reasons for high food prices.
2. If there is a food crisis in the world in the near future, it will be in the emerging economies.
Which of the above assumptions is/are valid ?
questions.subject: Comprehension

questions.context: A central message of modern development economics is the importance of income growth, by which is meant growth in Gross Domestic Product (GDP). In theory, rising GDP creates employment and investment opportunities. As incomes grow in a country where the level of GDP was once low, households, communities, and governments are increasingly able to set aside some funds for the production of things that make for a good life. Today GDP has assumed such a significant place in the development lexicon, that if someone mentions “economic growth”, we know they mean growth in GDP.
questions.stem:
With reference to the above passage, the following assumptions have been made :
1. Rising GDP is essential for a country to be a developed country.
2. Rising GDP guarantees a reasonable distribution of income to all households.
Which of the above assumptions is/are valid ?

questions.context: It is certain, that seditions, wars, and contempt or breach of the laws are not so much to be imputed to the wickedness of the subjects, as to the bad state of a dominion. For men are not born fit for citizenship, but must be made so. Besides, men’s natural passions are everywhere the same; and if wickedness more prevails, and more offences are committed in one commonwealth than in another, it is certain that the former has neither enough pursued the end of unity, nor framed its laws with sufficient forethought; and that, therefore, it has failed in making quite good its right as a commonwealth.
